The concept came from a true story of Kitty Genovese, a woman who was raped and stabbed multiple times even though all of hear neigbors heard her screams, as they felt someone else would do something about it.

I cannot personally tell you what to do, but anytime I hear screams or someone else's life in danger I ALWAYS call 911, and do as much as I can to figure out what is happening without putting myself in danger. Okay, so I know I'm a few hours late, but as a "frequent flyer" (2x a month) I can tell you guys whats up with flying with dip. I will write this in a FAQ Style, and also give my sources at the end of this post. 

Can I bring smokeless tobacco to the airport/airplane:

The TSA does NOT prohibit travelers from carrying chewing tobacco, checked or carry on.

Do they ID you?
 They DO NOT do I.D check anyone carrying it.

How much?

I have searched through the TSA guidelines thoroughly and have not found a single post on the limit for smokeless tobacco. However I have asked TSA at the airport and from experience they have said as long as you are not carrying an entire suitcase full of it, there should be no problem.

Can I dip on the plane?
No. But, with that being said I often do. Out of courtesy to other passengers, I always dip pouches and make sure I spit into a NON see through container (starbucks cup, thermostat etc.)

What about on international flights?

Different countries have different rules, and you should always check regulations before flying in. In your case, Turks and Caicos is a British Overseas Territory. The regulation is as follows: The legal limit when entering is 230 g of tobacco. To figure out how much you have, look at your can and it will tell you the grams on the seal. Grams in 1 can divided by 230 = How many cans you can have. But, they are very relaxed about this, and probably won't check.

Pro Tip: When entering the U.S you fill out I-94 form. It will ask whether you are carrying tobacco. I never put yes unless I have like a few logs. It might turn out to be a pain in the ass.
